```{r m1-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(postrank)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
```

A posterior distribution represents uncertainty about the targets, whereas
a grading rule determines which pairwise comparisons are disclosed. We
consider this decision for one criterion, using the loss implemented in
postrank. We then examine the restrictions imposed by an ordered grading
and establish the conditions under which the scalar problem has the same
minimizers as the report-card objective of Kline, Rose, and Walters (2024).

The [introductory article](a1-getting-started.html) describes the corresponding
analysis. Here the assumptions and the relationship between the objectives
are examined by finite enumeration, without model fitting or an
optimization backend.

## Targets and reporting actions {#targets-and-a-report-are-different-objects}

Let \(\theta_i\) denote the target for entity \(i\), oriented so that larger
values have higher reporting priority. Depending on the application,
priority may refer to a favorable outcome or to greater need for attention.
This interpretation is specified before grading. The supplied posterior is
a joint law for the targets, conditional on the observed information and
the model from which it was obtained.

A report assigns ordered integer grades \(g_i\). **Grade 1 has highest
priority**: \(g_i<g_j\) publishes that \(i\) is above \(j\).
The relation \(g_i=g_j\) withholds their comparison. It asserts neither
equal latent targets nor practical equivalence. Labels can be compressed
to consecutive occupied grades without changing any pair relation.

With \(n\) entities there are \(M=\binom n2\) unordered pairs. Let
\(N(g)\) be the number assigned different grades. Each disclosed pair has
one published direction, so it is counted once even when a formula sums
over ordered indices. For a fixed report, define

\[
e_{ij}=\Pr(\theta_i\leq\theta_j),\qquad
E(g)=\sum_{i\ne j}\mathbf1\{g_i<g_j\}e_{ij}.
\]

Thus \(E\) is the posterior expected number of wrong-direction disclosures.
The basic input domain requires zero probability of equality for every
distinct entity pair, giving \(e_{ij}+e_{ji}=1\). The diagonal is not a
comparison. Positive equality mass needs the separate interpretation and
input domain in [True ties and withheld comparisons](m4-ties-and-withholding.html).

## Directional-error and withholding loss {#price-a-wrong-direction-and-a-withheld-comparison}

An incorrect disclosed direction has cost one; withholding a pair has cost
\(\tau\). The normalized posterior expected loss is

\[
R_\tau(g)=\frac{E(g)+\tau\{M-N(g)\}}{M}.
\]

The public API accepts \(0<\tau\leq1/2\), with smaller values assigning a
lower cost to withholding. The parameter specifies a preference over
reporting consequences. It is therefore distinct from posterior
uncertainty, a confidence level, and a pair-specific error constraint.
A grade cap restricts the available reports without altering the loss.

The interpretation depends on the denominator. The quantity \(E/M\)
averages expected errors over all pairs, whereas \(E/N\), defined for
\(N>0\), averages over disclosed pairs. Risk additionally accounts for
withheld comparisons. An all-withheld report has \(N=0\), risk \(\tau\),
and undefined \(E/N\). This report is an admissible action and must be
distinguished from a computation that returns no grades.

For an isolated pair, the posterior expected costs are as follows:

| Action | Posterior expected cost |
|:--|:--|
| Publish \(i\) above \(j\) | \(e_{ij}\) |
| Publish \(j\) above \(i\) | \(e_{ji}=1-e_{ij}\) |
| Withhold the comparison | \(\tau\) |

For \(\tau<1/2\), a direction is uniquely preferred when its error probability
is below \(\tau\). When that error equals \(\tau\), publishing that direction
and withholding have equal expected cost. At \(e_{ij}=e_{ji}=\tau=1/2\), all three
actions tie. These comparisons solve the isolated-pair problem. A set of
such local decisions need not be expressible as grades.

## Pairwise decisions and coherent grades {#a-small-law-where-local-decisions-cannot-form-grades}

Consider three fictional entities A, B and C. Each row below specifies a
complete target state, and the associated masses define a finite joint
law. The states contain no latent equalities. The calculation therefore
uses the full law rather than a Monte Carlo approximation.

```{r m1-state-law}
states <- rbind(ABC = c(A = 3, B = 2, C = 1),
                ACB = c(A = 3, B = 1, C = 2),
                BAC = c(A = 2, B = 3, C = 1),
                CBA = c(A = 1, B = 2, C = 3))
mass_numerator <- c(12L, 3L, 3L, 2L)
probability <- mass_numerator / 20
knitr::kable(data.frame(State = rownames(states), states,
  Probability = probability), row.names = FALSE)
```

Summing the masses of states supporting each comparison gives the error
probabilities for publishing A above B, B above C, and A above C:

```{r m1-pair-errors}
ids <- colnames(states)
error <- matrix(NA_real_, 3, 3, dimnames = list(ids, ids))
for (i in 1:3) for (j in setdiff(1:3, i))
  error[i, j] <- sum(probability * (states[, i] <= states[, j]))
pairs <- data.frame(Direction = c("A above B", "B above C", "A above C"),
  Error = error[cbind(c(1, 2, 1), c(2, 3, 3))])
knitr::kable(pairs, row.names = FALSE)
```

Set \(\tau=1/5\). The local rule withholds A versus B and B versus C,
because their smaller directional error is \(1/4>1/5\), while it publishes
A above C, with error \(1/10\). But two shared grades would imply
\(g_A=g_B=g_C\). The local pattern is therefore infeasible as a grade
report, despite having a transitive majority order A above B above C.

This finite construction illustrates the phenomenon in KRW's Example 1
(pp. 2481–2482); their original example uses independent normal beliefs.
The companion theory's
[pair-versus-grade section](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/10-krw-foundation.html#sec-pair-versus-grade)
develops the finite example and its exact risks.

### Enumeration of coherent reports {#check-every-coherent-report}

For three labeled entities, the 13 ordered partitions can be enumerated
by retaining consecutive occupied labels. The calculation below sums
wrong-direction events over the complete states. It requires neither an
optimization backend nor independence of errors for different pairs.

```{r m1-enumerate}
actions <- as.matrix(expand.grid(A = 1:3, B = 1:3, C = 1:3))
keep <- apply(actions, 1, function(g)
  identical(sort(unique(as.integer(g))), seq_len(max(g))))
actions <- actions[keep, , drop = FALSE]
tau <- 1 / 5
lambda <- tau / (1 - tau)
counts <- function(g) {
  disclosed <- outer(g, g, "<")
  wrong <- apply(states, 1, function(theta)
    sum(disclosed & outer(theta, theta, "<=")))
  N <- sum(disclosed)
  E_numerator <- sum(mass_numerator * wrong)
  C_numerator <- 20 * N - E_numerator
  c(N = N, E_numerator = E_numerator,
    risk_numerator = 5 * E_numerator + 20 * (3 - N),
    krw_numerator = 4 * E_numerator - C_numerator)
}
exact <- t(apply(actions, 1, counts))
risk <- exact[, "risk_numerator"] / 300
krw_risk <- exact[, "krw_numerator"] / 240
best <- which(exact[, "risk_numerator"] == min(exact[, "risk_numerator"]))
result <- data.frame(Grades = apply(actions, 1, paste, collapse = "/"),
  N = exact[, "N"], E = exact[, "E_numerator"] / 20,
  E_over_N = ifelse(exact[, "N"] > 0,
    exact[, "E_numerator"] / (20 * exact[, "N"]), NA_real_),
  Risk = risk)
knitr::kable(result[order(result$Risk, result$Grades), ],
  digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

The integer numerators retain exact comparisons for this specified rational
example. Both **1/1/2 and 1/2/2** minimize risk at \(11/60\), approximately
`r fmt(min(risk))`. Each discloses two pairs, has expected error count
\(7/20\), and gives \(E/N=7/40\). One includes B above C and the other
A above B, each with error probability \(1/4\). Thus an individually disclosed
pair can have error greater than \(\tau\) in an optimal coherent report.

The infeasible set of pairwise decisions has average cost \(1/6\), which
is below the minimum over coherent reports by \(1/60\). It thus supplies
a lower bound from a relaxed problem, although it cannot itself be
represented by a grading. Since the coherent problem has two minimizers,
returning one grade vector would not establish uniqueness.

The same probabilities can be supplied to the package to evaluate each
fixed action. This numerical input is compared with the independent
reference calculation based on the finite law and its integer masses.

```{r m1-package-evaluation}
input <- postrank_probabilities(error, criterion = "priority",
  event = "directional_error", zero_ties = TRUE, margin = 0,
  source = list(kind = "analytic_reference",
    description = "Exact four-state enumeration with masses 12/20,3/20,3/20,2/20",
    conditioning = "The complete fixed finite target law shown in this article"),
  targets = c(priority = "Fictional target values; larger means higher reporting priority"))
evaluated <- apply(actions, 1, function(g)
  postrank_evaluate(setNames(g, ids), input,
    weights = c(priority = 1), tau = tau)$primary_risk)
max(abs(evaluated - risk))
```

`postrank_evaluate()` scores supplied grades; it does not check that they
obey an additional cap or error budget. Here all 13 actions belong to the
explicit unrestricted three-entity family by construction.

An aggregate inequality does follow if the all-withheld report is feasible
and \(g^*\) exactly minimizes this same posterior loss:

\[
R_\tau(g^*)\leq\tau\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
E(g^*)\leq\tau N(g^*).
\]

For positive disclosure this bounds the *average* posterior error fraction,
as \(7/40<1/5\) illustrates. An exact requirement of more than one occupied
grade excludes the all-withheld benchmark. Numerical optimization gaps and
Monte Carlo error also require separate treatment. The inequality is not
a bound for a different population law or proof that the model is calibrated.

## Correspondence with the scalar KRW objective {#match-the-scalar-krw-objective}

KRW rewards a correctly disclosed pair by \(\lambda\), penalizes an incorrect
pair by one, and gives a withheld pair payoff zero. Their original numerical
grades run in the opposite direction: larger \(d_i\) denotes more discrimination.
After reversing occupied labels, \(d_i=G+1-g_i\), both conventions publish
the same relations. Negating and averaging the pair payoffs gives the loss

\[
L_{K,\lambda}(g,\theta)=\{D_{<}(g,\theta)-\lambda C(g,\theta)\}/M,
\]

where \(D_{<}\) counts strictly wrong disclosed directions and \(C\) counts
correct ones. Their definitions and constrained formulation appear in
[Kline, Rose and Walters (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20230700),
Section II, pp. 2477–2482, equations (1)–(6).

Under zero pairwise equality probability, wrong and correct counts sum to
\(N\). Substitution gives

\[
\lambda=\frac{\tau}{1-\tau},\qquad
\tau=\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda},\qquad
R_\tau(g)=\tau+(1-\tau)R_{K,\lambda}(g).
\]

The positive multiplier preserves the **whole set of minimizers** when both
objectives use the same posterior, labeled entities, target directions and
nonempty action family. This applies to a shared restricted family as well
as to all ordered partitions; changing the family can change its optimum.
No independence of pair error indicators is needed.

```{r m1-affine-check}
max(abs(risk - (tau + (1 - tau) * krw_risk)))
identical(best, which(exact[, "krw_numerator"] == min(exact[, "krw_numerator"])))
c(tau = tau, lambda = lambda)
```

Thus \(\lambda=.25\) corresponds to \(\tau=.20\), rather than \(\tau=.25\).
The KRW risk can be negative because it rewards correct publication; its
raw scale is not the normalized withholding loss. The detailed
[affine derivation](https://joonho112.github.io/postrank-theory-book/chapters/10-krw-foundation.html#sec-scalar-reduction)
keeps the grade orientation, normalization and latent-equality condition explicit.

The algebraic endpoint \(\tau=0\) corresponds to \(\lambda=0\); it is outside
the current postrank API. At \(\tau=1/2\), \(\lambda=1\). An uncertain pair
with two equally likely strict orders then gives the same expected cost
for publication in either direction and for withholding. A fine grade at that boundary
does not by itself demonstrate strong evidence for its directions.

If latent equality has positive mass, strict and weak errors differ.
For a disclosed equality, the basic weak-error convention counts an error,
whereas both KRW strict counts are zero. An additional action-dependent term
then appears, so the displayed equivalence does not follow without further
conditions.
The [tie-aware article](m4-ties-and-withholding.html) describes the separate
equality-neutral route without changing the source paper's assumptions.

### Comparison between implementations {#compare-implementations-on-the-same-problem}

The scalar `gradepath::gp_grade()` procedure jointly optimizes the report.
Its unrestricted problem corresponds to postrank when both allow up to
\(n\) grades, impose no additional error-budget or exact-count constraint,
and use the corresponding parameter values, probability orientation and
target law. Optimizing contiguous cuts in a fixed score order is a more
restricted problem. Similarly, a smaller grade cap changes the feasible
family unless it is imposed in both implementations.

Probability floors and other adjustments can alter the coefficients and
must therefore be matched in comparisons between implementations. The
resulting pair relations and reevaluated losses provide the relevant
comparison. With multiple minimizers, different reports can attain the
same minimum. Neither a raw backend status nor agreement on one grading
establishes equality of the entire solution sets.

[Computing grades and choosing settings](m5-computing-grades.html)
describes fixed-order and joint optimization, together with incumbents,
lower bounds and numerical gaps.
[Several criteria and competing goals](m2-several-criteria.html) extends
the additive loss to multiple criteria and distinguishes composite targets.
The [school example](a2-cde-accountability.html) applies the single-criterion
analysis to uncertain absence probabilities.
